description: PROXIMA is a two-member team from Dhaka, Bangladesh. We combine AI, software engineering, data analysis and UI/UX design to explore space technology. Our interests include Mars exploration, autonomous navigation, mission planning and 3D visualization. We aim to build reliable solutions using NASA open data.
summary:
ARES PATHFINDER is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning platform developed by Team PROXIMA from Dhaka, Bangladesh, for NASA's “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge.

Exploring Mars requires more than identifying a destination. Astronauts must understand challenging terrain, manage limited resources, overcome hazards, and plan a safe return.

Our solution connects three experiences:

Mars Atlas visualizes NASA/USGS-derived Jezero terrain, scientific imagery, elevation, and historical observations.

Mission Ops uses A* pathfinding to compare routes, evaluate terrain hazards, and calculate simulated oxygen, energy, time, and return reserves.

Mars Odyssey introduces ten interactive 3D missions involving astronaut exploration, geological sampling, rover navigation, robotic operations, communication networks, rescue, polar science, and environmental survival.

Built as a browser-based educational prototype, ARES PATHFINDER connects real planetary data with explainable planning and interactive gameplay.

Our goal is to help students explore Mars, understand planetary science, develop problem-solving skills, and learn why every successful expedition must include a safe return.
details:
ARES PATHFINDER

Explore Mars. Understand the Terrain. Plan the Return.

1. Project Overview

ARES PATHFINDER is a browser-based Mars exploration, scientific mission-planning, and interactive 3D educational platform developed by Team PROXIMA from Dhaka, Bangladesh.

Created for NASA's “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge, the project combines NASA-derived Martian terrain data, explainable route planning, simulated mission resource management, and ten distinct interactive mission scenarios.

Our central question is:

How can future explorers navigate challenging Martian terrain, perform meaningful scientific tasks, manage limited resources, and return safely?

ARES PATHFINDER brings together three connected modules: Mars Atlas, Mission Ops, and Mars Odyssey.

The platform enables students to move beyond passive observation and participate in realistic-inspired mission decisions.

2. The Problem We Address

Mars presents significant challenges for human and robotic exploration.

Its surface contains steep slopes, impact craters, loose sand, rocky formations, deep canyons, and regions with limited observation coverage.

Future surface expeditions must also account for constrained oxygen, energy, communication, environmental exposure, scientific equipment, and the resources required for the return journey.

A route that appears shorter may be more dangerous or require more resources than a longer alternative.

Traditional planetary maps can communicate scientific information, but they do not necessarily help non-specialists experience the consequences of mission-planning decisions.

Our project addresses this educational gap by connecting planetary data, explainable navigation, and hands-on mission simulations.

3. Our Solution — Three Connected Experiences

A. MARS ATLAS — Scientific Planetary Exploration

Mars Atlas enables users to inspect Martian geographical regions and explore relevant scientific observations.

Its Jezero exploration experience incorporates supplied NASA/USGS-derived HiRISE digital terrain and optical imagery subsets.

Users can examine:

  • Martian surface terrain and geographical features.
  • Elevation, slope, and terrain roughness.
  • Optical imagery and mapped surface structures.
  • Scientific context and historical environmental observations.
  • Available data coverage and limitations.
  • 3D representations of supported locations.

The project also incorporates NASA Mars Trek planetary context, NASA image resources, and historical observational references.

Source-backed terrain is distinguished from reconstructed scenery, visual enhancements, and simulated environmental conditions.

B. MISSION OPS — Intelligent Navigation and Safe-Return Planning

Mission Ops uses the A pathfinding algorithm* to calculate and compare navigation options.

Instead of selecting a route based only on distance, the planning system considers terrain constraints, modeled environmental hazards, and mission resource budgets.

Its main functions include:

  • Terrain-aware route calculation.
  • Comparison of distance and hazard costs.
  • Slope and obstacle restrictions.
  • NoData and unavailable-terrain handling.
  • Simulated oxygen and energy consumption.
  • Mission time estimation.
  • Return-reserve analysis.
  • Route infeasibility detection.
  • Emergency replanning and mission abort decisions.
  • Contextual explanations of navigation choices.

The objective is to demonstrate that reaching a scientific destination is only one part of a successful expedition. The explorer must also preserve sufficient resources to return safely.

These calculations are educational simulations and are not certified for real astronaut operations.

C. MARS ODYSSEY — Ten Interactive 3D Mars Missions

Mars Odyssey transforms exploration and mission planning into a ten-stage interactive adventure.

Players select from six fictional astronaut characters:

Leon, Ethan, Orion, Sadia, Amelia, and Noor.

They can also use three robotic systems:

ATLAS-6: A ground rover for navigation, transporting equipment, and vehicle recovery.

SKYSCOUT: An aerial scouting system for investigating routes and locating mission targets.

ALPHA: A robotic utility system for manipulating equipment, repairing objects, and installing communication relays.

The campaign introduces increasingly complex scientific and engineering tasks.

Each stage has its own mission objectives, environmental challenges, player interactions, resource-management decisions, and progression rewards.

4. THE TEN MARS ODYSSEY MISSIONS

STAGE 01 — FIRST FOOTSTEPS

Region: Jezero Plains
Environment: Rocky Martian plains, shallow terrain depressions, scattered boulders, landing equipment, and a research habitat.

Scientific and Engineering Problem:

How can astronauts prepare for their first surface exploration, navigate unfamiliar terrain, perform a survey, and return before their resources become insufficient?

Interactive Mission:

Players perform simulated EVA suit checks, calibrate a compass, navigate toward a survey beacon, recover a dropped marker, deploy a survey tripod, and physically place a player-selected national flag.

They also capture a Martian panorama and evaluate their return route.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn the fundamentals of EVA preparation, navigation, scientific surveying, waypoint use, resource awareness, and safe-return decisions.

Mission Reward: Starter scanner and waypoint tool.

STAGE 02 — ANCIENT RIVER

Region: Jezero Delta
Environment: Layered sedimentary formations, ancient delta deposits, fractured rocks, geological outcrops, and eroded terrain.

Scientific Problem:

How can scientists investigate geological evidence of ancient water and determine which rock samples are most valuable for further study?

Interactive Mission:

Players examine three geological outcrops, compare visible rock layers, inspect available scientific evidence, and select a sampling location.

They use a simulated drilling mechanism to control tool alignment, pressure, and heat. Collected samples must be packaged, labeled, and transported safely.

Sampling errors, contamination, and limited equipment capacity influence mission outcomes.

Learning Outcome:

Students explore sedimentary geology, evidence-based sample selection, geological observation, scientific documentation, and sample-handling limitations.

Mission Reward: Sampling arm and archive kit.

STAGE 03 — SHIFTING DUNES

Region: Gale Crater Dunes
Environment: Wind-shaped sand dunes, loose surface material, dark sand deposits, dune crests, and unstable driving conditions.

Engineering Problem:

How can a robotic vehicle traverse loose Martian sand without becoming immobilized or exhausting its available energy?

Interactive Mission:

Players operate the ATLAS-6 ground rover, inspect terrain, and control steering and throttle.

A simulated traction challenge introduces wheel slippage. Players analyze vehicle telemetry, adjust driving behavior, select traction equipment, or change their route.

They then attach a towing cable, recover stranded equipment, and transport it back to the station.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn about robotic mobility, wheel traction, vehicle control, terrain-dependent navigation, power consumption, and recovery engineering.

Mission Reward: Sand wheels and traction module.

STAGE 04 — MINERAL HUNTER

Region: Nili Fossae
Environment: Fractured bedrock, rocky escarpments, geological exposures, and scientific mineral observation overlays.

Scientific Problem:

How can researchers identify promising mineral targets when observations have limited coverage and varying uncertainty?

Interactive Mission:

Players inspect candidate mineral regions and locate three geological outcrops.

Using a handheld scanner, they compare observations with available source-linked information or clearly labeled simulated readings.

They must classify candidate materials, recognize unsupported conclusions, place survey markers, and return safely.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn the purpose of spectral analysis, mineral exploration, scientific uncertainty, observation coverage, and evidence-based classification.

Mission Reward: Spectral analyzer.

STAGE 05 — VOLCANIC FRONTIER

Region: Elysium Planitia
Environment: Ancient volcanic plains, basaltic rocks, geological ridges, fractured terrain, and fissure-like formations.

Scientific and Engineering Problem:

How can explorers investigate volcanic geological structures and safely deploy scientific instruments across difficult terrain?

Interactive Mission:

Players map three geological features, inspect slopes and surface stability, and determine a feasible route across a modeled terrain obstacle.

They deploy a bridge or cable-assisted crossing mechanism, transport a thermal probe, anchor the instrument, and perform a simulated measurement task.

Improper equipment placement and excessive load can require correction or alternative planning.

Learning Outcome:

Students investigate Martian volcanism, basaltic terrain, instrument deployment, structural stability, and mission logistics.

Mission Reward: Thermal probe and reinforced tires.

STAGE 06 — LABYRINTH NETWORK

Region: Noctis Labyrinthus
Environment: Deep fractured valleys, narrow corridors, high canyon walls, shadowed passages, and communication blind spots.

Engineering Problem:

How can astronauts and robotic systems maintain communications when surrounding terrain obstructs direct signals?

Interactive Mission:

Players investigate signal coverage, identify communication dead zones, and scout suitable relay locations.

They operate the ALPHA utility robot to position communication beacons using an articulated manipulator arm.

Relay placement, line-of-sight obstruction, signal strength, and limited power influence the communication network.

Players must establish a working link and preserve a viable return route.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn about communication networks, line-of-sight propagation, relay placement, robotic manipulation, and signal restoration.

Mission Reward: Relay beacon and robotic arm extension.

STAGE 07 — CANYON RESCUE

Region: Valles Marineris
Environment: Massive canyon formations, steep cliffs, layered rocky walls, narrow passages, and a simulated emergency recovery site.

Engineering Problem:

How can explorers locate and recover a stranded robotic vehicle without exposing the rescue mission to unacceptable terrain and resource risks?

Interactive Mission:

Players receive an intermittent distress signal and compare possible rescue routes.

A SKYSCOUT reconnaissance vehicle can investigate suitable areas and identify the stranded rover.

Players navigate toward the recovery site, inspect damaged equipment, replace a power component or perform a simulated repair, and use a towing mechanism.

If a route becomes unsafe, they must replan and return with the recovered vehicle.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn robotic rescue planning, terrain-risk assessment, reconnaissance, mechanical recovery, route alternatives, and emergency resource management.

Mission Reward: Emergency recovery kit.

STAGE 08 — FROZEN FRONTIER

Region: Martian South Polar Region
Environment: Polar deposits, seasonal carbon-dioxide frost, pale surface layers, low solar illumination, and slippery modeled terrain.

Scientific Problem:

How can explorers investigate Martian polar conditions while managing reduced traction, extreme cold, and limited thermal energy?

Interactive Mission:

Players inspect modeled frost boundaries, consider sunlight conditions, and configure their simulated suit-heating schedule.

They navigate low-traction terrain, install a frost sensor, investigate surface layers, and manage equipment and thermal power.

Route selection and heating requirements affect whether they can safely complete the mission and return.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn about Martian polar science, seasonal frost, thermal constraints, energy trade-offs, instrument deployment, and mobility under cold conditions.

Mission Reward: Thermal suit module.

STAGE 09 — INTO THE DUST

Region: Modeled Martian Dust Emergency
Environment: Dust-filled basin, reduced visibility, atmospheric haze, difficult navigation, and simulated solar-power reduction.

Scientific and Engineering Problem:

How can a mission maintain navigation and protect its return reserves when atmospheric dust reduces visibility and limits energy generation?

Interactive Mission:

Players begin a mapping expedition and establish navigation waypoints.

A simulated dust event reduces visibility and changes power and navigation conditions.

Players compare compass and route information, deploy emergency markers, activate backup energy, and recalculate a safer return path.

They must decide whether to continue optional research or abandon it to preserve essential resources.

Learning Outcome:

Students learn about Martian dust hazards, navigation uncertainty, solar-energy limitations, backup systems, emergency route planning, and risk-aware decision-making.

Mission Reward: Emergency energy cell and marker system.

STAGE 10 — THE LAST EXPEDITION

Region: Fictional Multi-Region Mars Mission
Environment: A composite mission environment incorporating rocky plains, delta-like terrain, dunes, crater rims, canyon-inspired passages, and multiple scientific work areas.

Final Scientific and Engineering Problem:

How can multiple robotic systems and a human exploration team coordinate scientific objectives, resource allocation, environmental risk assessment, and a safe return within one complex expedition?

Interactive Mission — Five Acts:

Act 1: Mission Planning

Players review available research objectives, evaluate terrain constraints, select scientific priorities, and plan their expedition.

Act 2: Equipment and Resource Allocation

Players select an astronaut, configure mission equipment, allocate simulated oxygen and power resources, and assign roles to ATLAS-6, SKYSCOUT, and ALPHA.

Act 3: Scientific Operations

Players undertake multiple research tasks involving geological sampling, thermal or spectral investigation, robotic support, and communication relay installation.

Act 4: Environmental Emergency

A simulated environmental or communication hazard changes mission conditions. Players must reassess their route, resource reserves, and equipment strategy.

Act 5: Coordinated Safe Return

Players select a feasible return route, preserve essential resource reserves, manage robotic equipment, and coordinate the expedition's return to the habitat.

Learning Outcome:

This final mission combines planetary geology, robotic exploration, scientific investigation, route planning, communications, environmental hazard management, logistical reasoning, and mission safety.

Mission Reward: Pathfinder Master Explorer achievement and free-exploration progression.

5. INTERACTIVE GAMEPLAY AND USER EXPERIENCE

Mars Odyssey is designed around the following progression:

Explore → Discover → Solve → Execute → Return → Reward

Players are expected to do more than simply walk between checkpoints.

Mission interactions include scanning, collecting samples, controlling robotic vehicles, installing instruments, deploying markers, repairing equipment, and responding to changing mission conditions.

The game includes:

  • Third-person astronaut exploration.
  • Keyboard and on-screen movement controls.
  • A navigation minimap and compass.
  • Mission objectives and contextual instructions.
  • Oxygen, energy, and return-reserve displays.
  • Context-sensitive interaction controls.
  • Robotic vehicle operation.
  • Scientific tools and equipment.
  • Mission checkpoints and saved progress.
  • Stage unlocking and fictional in-game rewards.
  • Failure explanations, retries, and recovery options.

These systems demonstrate how scientific observation, engineering decisions, and return planning can become part of interactive education.

6. TECHNOLOGIES AND DEVELOPMENT TOOLS

The submitted repository uses a browser-based technical architecture.

Frontend and 3D Rendering

  • JavaScript and web technologies.
  • Three.js and WebGL2.
  • Vite development and build tools.
  • glTF/GLB 3D models and physically based materials.

Game and Simulation Systems

  • Custom A* route-planning logic.
  • Terrain and obstacle constraints.
  • Mission resource simulation.
  • Character movement and skeletal animation.
  • Rover, drone, and robotic-arm interactions.
  • Locally saved campaign progress.
  • Web Audio for gameplay and environmental cues.

Backend and Data Processing

  • Python-based local server and NASA data gateway.
  • NASA/USGS terrain and imagery processing.
  • Processed local terrain tiles and data snapshots.
  • Scientific metadata and source attribution.

Development and Testing

  • Git and GitHub.
  • Blender and 3D asset preparation tools.
  • Automated JavaScript and Python checks.
  • Reproducible mission and route tests.

The implementation incorporates externally sourced, appropriately credited NASA 3D assets, planetary observations, and open-licensed visual resources.

7. WHAT MAKES ARES PATHFINDER CREATIVE?

ARES PATHFINDER connects three normally separate educational activities:

Scientific observation: Understanding planetary surface features through available NASA-derived geographical data.

Mission decision-making: Comparing routes and simulated resource constraints through explainable algorithms.

Interactive learning: Applying these decisions in fictional astronaut and robotic mission scenarios.

Its educational value comes from connecting the map, the route, and the player's actions.

For example, a route selected in Mission Ops can influence mission navigation, while hazardous terrain and resource limitations create meaningful decisions inside the exploration experience.

The ten missions introduce increasingly complex concepts, from basic surface surveying to coordinated robotic rescue and final expedition planning.

8. EXPECTED EDUCATIONAL IMPACT

ARES PATHFINDER is intended for students, STEM educators, robotics enthusiasts, and learners interested in planetary exploration.

The project aims to:

  • Make NASA planetary datasets easier to explore.
  • Introduce geological and environmental science concepts.
  • Demonstrate pathfinding and resource-constrained planning.
  • Teach practical robotics and navigation concepts.
  • Encourage evidence-based decision-making.
  • Connect space exploration to interactive STEM education.
  • Increase interest in planetary science, software engineering, robotics, and mission systems.

By combining visual exploration with interactive scientific challenges, the platform aims to make difficult concepts more understandable and engaging.

9. SCIENTIFIC ACCURACY AND LIMITATIONS

Scientific transparency is an essential part of ARES PATHFINDER.

The submitted codebase documents NASA/USGS-derived Jezero terrain and imagery subsets used in Mars Atlas, Mission Ops, and the first two missions. The processed terrain uses a different resolution from the original source products.

Stages 03–10 use geographically inspired reconstructed or modeled environments rather than claiming continuous high-resolution NASA-measured terrain.

Environmental hazards, oxygen and battery budgets, communication failures, and astronaut safety calculations are educational simulations.

Historical NASA atmospheric and audiovisual observations are distinguished from simulated live-game conditions.

The multi-region final mission is a fictional composite environment, not a single continuous NASA-surveyed landscape.

The repository contains ten authored mission scenarios and automated test documentation. However, automated checks do not establish that every stage has passed full-duration manual gameplay testing, independent terrain validation, mobile/VR acceptance, or final photorealistic quality review.

ARES PATHFINDER is therefore presented as an educational research prototype, not a NASA-certified navigation or astronaut safety system.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Team PROXIMA used ChatGPT (OpenAI) for research assistance, technical planning, coding support, debugging, documentation, and presentation preparation. AI image-generation tools were used for visual concepts and promotional design. NASA scientific data is distinguished from AI-generated visuals and simulated mission environments. AI-assisted work and third-party resources are acknowledged in the public GitHub repository.

10. CONCLUSION

ARES PATHFINDER demonstrates how NASA-derived planetary information, intelligent route-planning algorithms, and interactive 3D mission scenarios can be combined into one educational platform.

Through Mars Atlas, Mission Ops, and the ten-stage Mars Odyssey campaign, the project invites students to investigate the Red Planet, practice scientific reasoning, operate simulated robotic systems, and understand the importance of mission safety.

Our vision is to make Mars exploration more accessible through interactive learning—empowering future explorers to explore, discover, make decisions, and plan the return.

Team PROXIMA — Dhaka, Bangladesh.
